When an individual executes a series of signings during a single, continuous period of controlled system access, the first signing uses all components and subsequent signings use at least one component that only that individual can execute and that is designed for use only by that individual. Signings not performed during a single, continuous period of controlled access each use all components. E-signatures are used only by their genuine owners, and are administered so that attempted use by anyone other than the owner requires the collaboration of two or more individuals. Biometric e-signatures are designed so they cannot be used by anyone other than their genuine owners.
system_implications: The signing dialog re-authenticates at the moment of signing (user ID + password, or an SSO step-up with a second factor). The 'continuous period of controlled access' is defined strictly: any lock, timeout, logout or terminal switch ends it. Recommendation: require both components for all critical signatures (verification, QA review, release, MBR approval), because shop-floor terminals are shared. A verifier signs in the same dialog with their own full credentials; the performer's session can never supply the verifier's signature. No 'remember password'. Administrators cannot see passwords, and admin-set passwords force a change at first use (so misuse needs collusion). Biometric options, such as badge plus fingerprint in cleanrooms where typing is impractical, need liveness and anti-spoofing evidence.
verification_test: Sign twice in one session -> the second signing requires at least the password. After timeout or lock -> both components required. Try to record a verifier signature using the performer's session -> requires the verifier's own ID and password. An admin-reset password cannot be used to sign before it is changed.

requirement: Controls include: (a) keeping each combined ID code and password unique so no two individuals share the same combination; (b) periodically checking, recalling or revising ID code and password issuances (e.g., password aging); (c) loss-management procedures to electronically deauthorize lost, stolen, missing or compromised tokens, cards and other devices, and to issue replacements under suitable, rigorous controls; (d) transaction safeguards to prevent unauthorized use of passwords and/or ID codes, and to detect and report any attempted unauthorized use in an immediate and urgent manner to the system security unit and, as appropriate, organizational management; (e) initial and periodic testing of tokens or cards that bear or generate ID or password information, to ensure they work and have not been altered without authorization. Items (a)-(d) were confirmed verbatim; (e) is from the regulation text.
system_implications: Password policy: complexity, history, and aging or a documented risk-based equivalent (e.g., NIST SP 800-63B with compromised-password screening), with the rationale recorded. Account lockout after N failed login or signature attempts. Real-time security alerting (SIEM) on repeated failures, signature attempts on locked accounts, and anomalous access, routed to the security unit with acknowledgment tracking and escalation to management. Immediate revocation of lost badges or tokens, with replacement issued only after identity verification. Periodic badge and token functional tests.
verification_test: N failed signature attempts -> the account locks and an alert reaches the security unit within the defined minutes. A revoked badge cannot authenticate. Token test records exist.

source: FDA 'Guide to Inspections of Lyophilization of Parenterals' (July 1993); 21 CFR 211.137(c)
clause: Lyophilization cycle and controls; cycle validation; lyophilizer sterilization
requirement: The FDA investigator guide covers the lyophilization cycle and its controls, cycle validation, and lyophilizer sterilization and design. Records of cycle data are reviewed against the validated/filed cycle (details are from recollection; the guide is a 1993 inspection reference, not a guidance). For reconstituted products, labeling bears both reconstituted and unreconstituted expiration information (211.137(c)).
system_implications: Integrate the lyophilizer SCADA/historian: recipe ID and version, and per-phase setpoints and actuals (shelf temperature, chamber pressure, condenser temperature, product thermocouple/wireless probe temperatures, pressure-rise or comparative pressure tests, phase durations). Record loading pattern and time, stoppering, and chamber sterilization/leak-test status before loading. Excursions against validated ranges auto-create deviations. Loading/unloading times feed time-limit timers. Store native cycle data as dynamic records (US-DI-08).
verification_test: Replay a cycle file with a shelf-temperature excursion -> deviation created. A chamber with no valid SIP/leak test -> loading blocked.

source: Composite requirement (derived): 21 CFR 210.3 (lot number = complete history), 211.184(c), 211.188(b)(3), 211.130(c), 211.192 (extend investigation to associated batches/products), 211.150/211.196 (distribution for recall), 211.182 (equipment use sequence), 201.18, DSCSA 581/582 (serial -> lot; aggregation)
clause: Bidirectional genealogy and traceability across materials, equipment, rooms, people, time, packaging hierarchy and distribution
requirement: The regulations collectively require that, for any lot, the complete manufacturing, control, packing, holding and distribution history can be determined (backward trace), and that from any component lot, equipment, discrepancy or failure all associated batches, other products and consignees can be identified (forward trace and impact analysis for investigations and recalls). DSCSA adds package-level serial identity and parent-child aggregation that must map back to the lot and batch record.
system_implications: This answers the user's question on graph-based data structures and databases; the recommendation below is engineering judgment, not regulatory text. Genealogy is inherently a directed, time-stamped multigraph. Nodes: material lots, sublots/containers, batches/steps, equipment units, rooms, persons, sterilizer loads, EM samples, serial numbers, cases, pallets, shipments, consignees, deviations. Edges: consumed-by, produced, split/merge, used-equipment, performed-by, sterilized-in, aggregated-into, shipped-in, relates-to-investigation. Queries are variable-depth (multi-stage API -> granulate -> tablets -> coated -> packaged; rework; blending of several intermediate lots; inter-site transfers), so graph modelling fits naturally. The same regulations also require ACID transactional hard stops (211.84, 211.101), an immutable append-only audit trail (11.10(e)), signatures cryptographically bound to record content (11.70), backup and restore as true copies (211.68(b)), retention of 10+ years with readable exports (11.10(b),(c); 211.180), and full validation (211.68, 11.10(a)). Recommended pattern: (1) The system of record is an ACID store (relational, e.g., PostgreSQL, or equivalent) with an append-only, hash-chained event/transaction ledger. Genealogy edges are written in the same transaction as the business event (e.g., a consumption record), so the graph can never disagree with the batch record and there is no dual-write inconsistency. (2) Most genealogy queries run fine as recursive queries (SQL recursive CTEs, or SQL/PGQ property-graph queries where the RDBMS supports them) on indexed edge tables. DSCSA aggregation is shallow (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) but high-volume (millions of serials per batch), which relational parent-pointer tables handle well. (3) If scale or latency across many sites needs a dedicated graph database for investigation or recall analytics, make it a derived, read-only, rebuildable projection (CQRS) fed from the ledger via outbox/CDC. Add automated reconciliation (edge counts and hashes per lot) and treat it as GMP-relevant, validated software if its outputs drive GMP decisions such as investigation scope or recall lists. Never make it the sole store of signed records unless it provides equivalent Part 11 audit trail, immutability, point-in-time recovery and long-term export, which most graph databases do not offer natively. (4) Keep genealogy bitemporal (valid time and recording time), so the graph 'as known at release' can be reconstructed after later corrections. (5) Use globally unique IDs with site-scoped business lot numbers to support multi-site graphs, and partition operational data by site with a global genealogy index. 211.180(c) permits central electronic retrieval. (6) The MBR/recipe structure (ISA-88 procedure -> unit procedure -> operation -> phase, with parallel branches) is a DAG that can live as versioned structured documents inside the relational store; it does not require a graph database.
verification_test: (a) Backward and forward trace for seeded complex scenarios (split, merge, rework, inter-site transfer, repack) returns the exact expected node sets. (b) Reconciliation job: the graph projection (if used) equals ledger-derived edges for 100% of lots, and any drift raises an alert. (c) Impact query performance: forward trace from a high-usage excipient lot across 3 years and N sites completes within the SLA. (d) Point-in-time query reproduces the genealogy as of the release timestamp after a later correction. (e) Rebuild the projection from the ledger in a test environment and compare hashes.

clause: Record integrity architecture: immutability, contemporaneous commit, timestamps, signature binding
requirement: Records must be attributable and contemporaneous, changes must not obscure prior values, audit trails must be computer-generated, time-stamped and retained as long as the record, signatures must be inseparably linked to the records they sign, and backups must be exact and secure from alteration or loss.
system_implications: Engineering judgment derived from the cited rules. Use an event-sourced or append-only versioned record store for GMP data: each entry is an immutable event carrying user, device, UTC server timestamp, site time zone, reason for any change, and a content hash chained to the previous event. The 'current' batch record view is a projection of these events. Signatures reference the hash of the exact record version. A trusted time source (NTP stratum with drift monitoring) must be used, and time-sync failures are alarms. Clock drift on edge devices beyond a threshold blocks data capture. Store UTC and render site-local time with offset (important for multi-site and daylight-saving changes). Database administrators must not be able to alter GMP tables without detection (separation of DBA duties, database activity monitoring, hash verification).
verification_test: Daylight-saving transition test: events around the change keep a correct order and correct displayed local times. Simulated NTP failure raises an alarm and stops capture on edge devices past the drift threshold. DBA-level update is detected by hash verification and database activity monitoring.
